HART 102.name: Introduction to Research Skills
HART 102.description: Examination of a theme concerning the art, architecture, and archaeology of the Mediterranean basin and the Near East, with emphasis on developing the skills essential for successful university study: reading scholarly works, taking notes, identifying research problems, writing papers (both short reports and longer research papers), giving oral presentations, and taking part in discussions. The topic examined will vary from year to year, depending on the interests of the instructor.

HART 111.name: Introduction to Archaeology
HART 111.description: This course provides background material essential for any student of archaeology, covering such topics as the history of archaeological research and excavation, major archaeological discoveries of past centuries, modern excavating, surveying and recording techniques, dating methods, identification of sites and the topographical factors involved in locating ancient settlements.

HART 117.name: Ways of Seeing: Approaches to Art and Architectural History
HART 117.description: A thematic introduction to great works of art and architecture, techniques of analysis, and methods of interpretation. Examples studied will be taken from cultures around the world, ancient, medieval, and modern, with the majority coming from the western tradition. Themes explored will include: form; style; iconography (the subject matter of art); images of the sacred; architecture and ritual; politics and art; landscapes and natural settings; private architecture: the house; and perspectives from sociology, Marxism, feminism, and semiotics.

HART 120.name: Human Evolution and World Prehistory
HART 120.description: This course is a survey of the human prehistory of Africa, Europe and Asia from the first hominids to the Mesolithic period, with particular emphasis on morphological evolution, environment and cultural developments.

HART 125.name: Archaeological Illustration
HART 125.description: This course provides students with the basic principles and practical skills of archaeological illustration, from the elementary field level, for record purposes, leading up to drawings made to final publication standard. The coursework includes preparing and finishing drawings of the usual range of artefacts recovered during an excavation, such as pottery, metalwork, stonework, and modified animal bone.

HART 126.name: Fieldwork Methodologies in Archaeology
HART 126.description: The course aims at providing students with the fundamental tools to navigate their first experiences in archaeological fieldwork, both in survey and excavation contexts. The classes are designed to offer both the necessary conceptual background to fieldwork research, and the technical aspects of daily activities in a project, showcasing in particular the use of digital approaches to data documentation and analysis.

HART 206.name: Mythologies of the Ancient Mediterranean World
HART 206.description: Introduction to mythologies of the Mesopotamian, Egyptian and Greco-Roman civilizations, from a comparative and cultural perspective. This course will survey the major myths about gods, goddesses, heroes and heroines, and consider the role they fulfilled in the societies that created them. Lectures will be supplemented by visual material and ancient written sources.

HART 208.name: Roman Art and Archaeology
HART 208.description: This course examines the origins and development of Roman art and architecture in its archaeological setting from the Etruscan period through to the reign of the emperor Constantine. The course focuses on the evidence from Rome and Italy, but also looks at the impact and influence of Rome on local art and architecture in the various provinces of the Roman Empire. Throughout the course an emphasis is placed on understanding the role of art and architecture in the Roman World in general, and in particular its use as a form of political propaganda.

HART 212.name: Introduction to Classical Archaeology
HART 212.description: This course surveys major aspects of the materials cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome, beginning with the Iron Age of Greece and concluding with the decline of the Western Roman Empire: their architecture, their arts, their economic and social development in urban and rural settings, as well as the way in which scholars have approached the field over its history. Equal weight is given to the development of Classical Greece, its Hellenistic expansion, and the Roman domination of the Mediterranean.

HART 219.name: Anatolia I-Hunters,Farmers,Merchants in Prehistoric Anatolia
HART 219.description: An introduction to the pre- and early historic archaeological heritage of Turkey, from the Early Neolithic (ca. 10.000 BC) to the advanced Iron Age (ca. 500 BC). Besides iconic places like Gobekli Tepe, Troia, Hattusa and Gordion, also less well known arenas of human action and interaction are surveyed.

HART 221.name: Great Discoveries from the Ancient World
HART 221.description: Archaeology can be defined as the study of human activity through the recovery and analysis of material culture, the things people living in past times have left behind them which we use to better understand earlier times. These "things" range from the objects they used in everyday life to their monuments and even their preserved bodies. This course examines how the method of archaeology originated and how it has developed up to the present day by analysing a series of "Great Discoveries" from the well-known, such as the discovery of Troy or of Tutanhkamun's grave, to less well-known examples, as with the finding of the Hoxne hand-axes and the grave of Richard III of England. In doing so the course will present the wide range of scientific methods used in archaeology today

HART 222.name: From Villages to Empires in Ancient Mesopotamia
HART 222.description: The goal of the course is to provide students with a long-term perspective on the change and continuity of Mesopotamian societies between the late Epipalaeolithic and the Iron Age (ca 11000-300 BCE). Topics include fundamental themes of Near Eastern archaeology such as sedentism, animal and plant domestication, power ideology, urbanization, state formation, and social stratification, as well as key archaeological sites, material culture and technology.

HART 225.name: Cultural Anthropology
HART 225.description: An introduction to cultural anthropology. Topics examined include the concept of culture; ethnographic research, its history, methods, and theory; language and communication; social identity, personality, and gender; subsistence patterns; economic systems; sex, marriage, and family; kinship and descent; grouping by age, common interest, and social status; political systems; religion and spirituality; the arts; and processes of cultural change.

HART 227.name: Greek Archaeology
HART 227.description: This course surveys major aspects of the material culture of Ancient Greece, beginning with the Iron Age of Greece and concluding with the Roman Empire: the architecture, the arts, the economic and social development in urban and rural settings, as well as the new interpretations in the light of the recent discoveries.

HART 228.name: UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Turkey-Göbeklitepe, Çatalhöyük, Troia and Hattusha
HART 228.description: This course aims to introduce the students to four iconic sites in Turkey, which all obtain a special position due to their inclusion in the UNESCO World Heritage canon. These "model sites", which are all very different in date, size and function, will be thoroughly surveyed, also in scope of their modern cultural and political significance. Suitable for archaeology and non-archaeology students alike.

HART 231.name: Ancient Greek I
HART 231.description: Introduction to ancient Greek for beginning students. The course will emphasize vocabulary acquisition grammar and reading.

HART 232.name: Ancient Greek II
HART 232.description: Continuation of the grammar and vocabulary acquisition started in Ancient Greek I.

HART 239.name: Latin I
HART 239.description: Introduction to Latin for beginning students. The course will emphasize both grammar and reading.

HART 240.name: Latin II
HART 240.description: Completion of the grammar and vocabulary acquisition begun in Latin I.

HART 303.name: Greek Sculpture
HART 303.description: The course will concentrate on the development of Greek sculpture with special emphasis on the state of research, on new interpretations of images and on the methodology of interpretation.

HART 305.name: Byzantine and Islamic Art and Archaeology
HART 305.description: A survey of art, architecture, and archaeology of the Mediterranean and Near East in the medieval and early modern periods, from Constantine the Great to the 15th century. Focus will be on the art and architecture of the Late Roman and Byzantine empires in Italy and the eastern Mediterranean basin and of early Islamic states.

HART 306.name: Hellenistic and Roman Sculpture
HART 306.description: An analytical survey of Hellenistic and Roman sculpture from the time of Alexander the Great to that of Constantine the Great (ca 300 BC-AD 300), this course looks at the techniques and materials sculptors used during the period, and the range of topics they depicted, from portraiture to historical narratives, as well as the stylistic changes and approaches made in this time span.

HART 307.name: Monumental Painting
HART 307.description: The arts of wall painting and mosaics in the Greek world and Italy from the Archaic period to the third century AD.

HART 308.name: Greek Vase Painting
HART 308.description: A survey of Greek vase painting from the Geometric period (ca. 9th century BC) to the 4th century BC with special attention to Attic vase painting of the Archaic and Classical periods.

HART 310.name: Introduction to Digital Archaeology
HART 310.description: Digital is omnipresent in all aspects of our lives and so it is also in all the archaeological disciplines. This course offers an overview of digital tools and methods used for the representation of our non-digital past, including basics of data organization and analyses, 3D modelling and virtual reality.

HART 311.name: GIS Applications in Archaeology
HART 311.description: This course offers an in-depth conceptual and practical introduction to Geographic Information Systems (GIS), a powerful suite that allows to digitally record excavation and survey projects, analyze remote sensing data (e.g. satellite, drone, geophysical data) and investigate human-environment interaction, relations between communities, and intra-site distribution of artefacts. Class topics include digitalization of data, mapping tools and analytical tools that will help students in their own research.

HART 313.name: European Prehistory
HART 313.description: Survey of European prehistory, from the time of Archaic humans to the first millennium BC. Paleolithic and Mesolithic cultures; Neolithic and Bronze Age cultures.

HART 315.name: Greek Architecture
HART 315.description: A survey of Greek building from ca. 700 BC to the 1st century BC. The Greek architectural tradition and its historical development will be emphasized (the history and nature of Doric and Ionic orders and of "Aeolic" and Corinthian styles). Materials, techniques and procedures of construction will also be covered. Sanctuary architecture provides the core material of the course but military, funerary, and ceremonial monuments will also be considered.

HART 316.name: Roman Architecture
HART 316.description: A survey of Roman architecture from its origins in the Iron Age to the Constantinian period (ca. 500 BC - AD 300), the course examines in detail the materials and methods used by Roman architects and the buildings they made in Rome and Italy and in the provinces of the Roman Empire.

HART 317.name: Archaeology of Troy
HART 317.description: A broad-based investigation into the problem of the origin and development of the Homeric city of Troy. The written and archaeological sources and the extent and the limitations of the data will be emphasized. The class will discuss the relationships between epic, history and archaeological evidence.

HART 318.name: Archaeology of Syria and Palestine
HART 318.description: The archaeology of the Levant and its relationship with surrounding cultures from the beginning of urban civilization to ca. 1200 BC.

HART 322.name: Orientalizing Period
HART 322.description: The orientalizing period (between roughly the late 8th and early 6th century BC) witnesses the renewal of extensive contacts between Greece and the Aegean world with Near Eastern civilizations. This course examines the forms of interaction between the Greek world and the East and the cultural transformation that followed.

HART 325.name: Anatolia II- The World of Hittites
HART 325.description: The course aims to paint an impressionistic understanding of the Hittite world in Anatolia between ca 1950 BCE and 700 BCE. It will on one side examine the deeds of important historical figures and their relations with their neighboring -and often adversary- states of Mycenae, Egypt, Mitanni and Babylon. In the process, it will discuss events like the Battle of Qadesh, the Trojan War, the Sea People and the so-called "collapse " of the Hittite Empire. On the other side, it will combine archaeological, historical and philological research to attempt reconstructing daily life in the Hittite kingdom, from craft to farming, from medicine to religious festivals.

HART 328.name: The Aegean Bronze Age
HART 328.description: The prehistoric cultures of the Aegean area, concentrating on Minoan Crete, Troy, the Aegean Islands, and Mycenaean Greece.

HART 330.name: Egyptian Art and Archaeology
HART 330.description: A survey of the art and archaeology of ancient Egypt, from the Predynastic Period to the end of the New Kingdom (4000-1100 BC). The course will emphasize major monuments of architecture, sculpture, relief and painting. Questions of stylistic change and historical context will be considered, as well as cultural relations with neighboring civilizations.

HART 333.name: Ancient Greek III
HART 333.description: Completion of the grammar and vocabulary acquisition started in Ancient Greek I and II.

HART 334.name: Ancient Greek IV
HART 334.description: Selections from Greek literature (such as Homer, Hesiod, Xenophon Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Plato, Herodotus and Thucydides). Also, an introduction to Epigraphy.

HART 335.name: Monuments of Babylon
HART 335.description: Babylon, named The Gate of the Gods, was by 600 BC the ancient world's largest city, and home to two of its "ancient wonders." Situated in today's southern Iraq, Babylon's urban plan, palaces, temples, museums, housing and lifestyle are known from the Greek historian Herodotus and other visitors, from the Old Testament, from Babylonian texts, and especially from a century of excavations at the site and its surroundings. The course will examine major aspects of this remarkable ancient city, with a focus on balancing the written and archaeological evidence.

HART 339.name: Introduction to Bioarchhaeology
HART 339.description: Bioarchaeology, archaeobotany, zooarchaeology, human-environment interactions, palaeoenvironment reconstruction, human osteoarchaeology, mortuary archaeology, anatomy, dentition, dietary habits, extra-masticatory use, palaeodemography, palaeopathology, traumatic injuries, habitual activities.

HART 342.name: Hittite Grammar I
HART 342.description: Hittite Grammar I introduces students to the grammar of Hittite, the oldest attested Indo-European language. Students will learn to read uncomplicated Hittite sentences and passages in transliteration and become familiar with the research tools of the field.

HART 343.name: Latin III
HART 343.description: Completion of the grammar points of the Latin language and an introduction to original texts. Also, an introduction to Epigraphy.

HART 344.name: Latin IV
HART 344.description: Readings and discussions of many of the works of Roman literature. Emphasis will be on correct translation of the Latin, with attention to genre and narrative technique, and to building facility in reading Latin. Selections from writers such as Plautus, Vergil, Cicero, Caesar, Lucretius, Petronius and Ovid will be read in the original.

HART 346.name: Daily Life in Ancient Greece
HART 346.description: The daily life of ancient Greeks is examined, from birth and childhood to death, from morning to evening into night, with differences according to gender, age, and social class. Houses and other buildings, sculpture, vase painting, mosaics, and miscellaneous objects from houses and tombs provide the evidence for this look at ancient Greek society.

HART 348.name: Coloring Greek and Roman Antiquity: Mosaics, Paintings and Sculptures
HART 348.description: This course will focus on Greek and Roman mosaics, paintings and sculptures to show the importance given to colors and the mastery of artists who worked with them. It will also examine why modern scholarship on classical statuary white-washed its polychromy and the recent rediscovery of colors thanks to new technologies.

HART 351.name: Monuments of Athens
HART 351.description: The monuments of Athens from the Archaic period through the Hellenistic and Roman periods, considering stylistic developments and historical and cultural context.

HART 352.name: Monuments of Rome
HART 352.description: A detailed study of the main monuments of ancient Rome from its origins to the early Christian period (ca 500 BC - AD 500), with an emphasis on their characteristics and their role and function in everyday life.

HART 353.name: Introduction to Akkadian
HART 353.description: Introduction to Akkadian for beginning students. No previous knowledge of a foreign language is needed. The course is particularly recommended to archaeology students whose interests lie in Bronze Age Mesopotamia and Anatolia.

HART 354.name: Akkadian II
HART 354.description: This course will focus on the study of Old Babylonian texts, developing translation skills and examining the texts within their historical context. Emphasis will be given to the translation of selected readings.

HART 355.name: Akkadian III
HART 355.description: This course is a continuation of Akkadian I and II, with an emphasis on readings from ancient Near Eastern literature from different dialects/scripts/periods of Akkadian.

HART 356.name: Akkadian IV
HART 356.description: This course is a continuation of Akkadian I and Akkadian III. It will focus on readings on readings from ancient Near Eastern literature from different dialects/scripts/periods of Akkadian.

HART 357.name: Akkadian I
HART 357.description: Introduction to Akkadian for beginning students. The course is recommended to Archaeology students whose interests lie in Bronze Age Mesopotamia and Anatolia.

HART 360.name: Ancient Mesoamerican Civilizations
HART 360.description: A survey of the civilizations of Mesoamerica from earliest human settlement to the Spanish conquest, with emphasis on the art and archaeology of the great states: Olmec, Teotihuacan, Maya, Toltec, and Aztec.

HART 365.name: Ancient Cities
HART 365.description: A study of urban developments from the Neolithic period onwards, covering in particular cities of the Near East, Egypt, the Aegean, Greece and the Roman world.

HART 366.name: The Buried Cities of Campania
HART 366.description: This course provides a detailed analysis of Pompeii and Herculaneum, two Italian cities in the Campania region of Italy buried by the volcanic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. Re-discovered in the 18th century, excavations at both places have provided much evidence regarding the art and architecture and the everyday life of the region in the Republican and early Imperial periods. The first part of the course will examine the history of both cities up to the time of the eruption in AD 79 and will introduce you to their public and private architecture. The second part will examine in more detail what these sites tell us about everyday life there at the time of the eruption, and in particular the ways in which the residents lived, worked and played, which will allow you to better conceptualise patterns of life in the two places in the period between c. 150 BC - AD 79.

HART 367.name: Pompeii: Life and Death of a Roman City
HART 367.description: In this course we will look at what has been learnt from archaeology about Pompeii, a town in central Italy buried with many of its inhabitants still there by the eruption of the Mount Vesuvius volcano in AD 79. After examining the history of the site and its' public and private architecture up to the time of the eruption, we will examine in more detail the public, social, private and economic life of the place, as learnt from excavation and various scientific approaches, such as DNA and biomolecular analyses of bodies and of food remains, that combine to give a holistic view of Pompeii from 150 BC to the day of its burial in AD 79.

HART 370.name: Iron Age Sculpture of the Near East
HART 370.description: Attention is focused on the major sculptural groups of the Anatolians, Assyrians, Neo-Babylonians and Persians.

HART 372.name: Hittite I
HART 372.description: An introduction to Hittite, the oldest attested Indo-European language. Overview of the discovery of the Hittite language and civilization, and presentation of the basics of Hittite grammar and cuneiform script.

HART 373.name: Hittite II
HART 373.description: A detailed survey of Hittite grammar and orthography. Beginner level excerpts from Hittite texts will be read and analyzed.

HART 374.name: Hittite III
HART 374.description: This course will offer a survey of the Hittite textual corpus. Students will read and translate selected historical and religious texts.

HART 375.name: Hittite IV
HART 375.description: This course will further explore the Hittite text corpus. Students will read and translate selected literary texts.

HART 376.name: The Land of a Thousand Gods: History and Literature of Ancient Anatolia
HART 376.description: This course will survey the history and literature of early Anatolian civilizations such as the Hittites, Phrygians, and Urartians, from the Early Bronze Age (c. 3000 BCE) to the end of the Persian Period (c. 330 BCE). Students will explore the history of Anatolia through a diverse range of theoretical lectures and hands-on activities: reading and interpreting primary sources (myths, annals, treaties, letters, etc.) in English translation, visiting museums and archaeological sites, or participating in workshops on ancient writing techniques.

HART 380.name: Archaeology of Phoenicia
HART 380.description: Detailed survey of Phoenician art and archaeology in its historical and economic context. There will be particular emphasis on the influences and relationships, especially in the fields of trade and art, between the Phoenicians and the rest of the Mediterranean and Near Eastern World.

HART 399.name: Summer Practice I
HART 399.description: A course in which the students is expected to take part in actual field work preferably on an excavation or in a museum; other options possible, with approval from department. A report of performance to be submitted to the Department by the supervisor of the field project.

HART 400.name: Senior Project
HART 400.description: A project on a specific topic in an area of archaeology, the history of ancient art, museum studies or ancient history to be carried out by the student or a group of students under the supervision of the project coordinator. The form of the project is free, and may consist of any of the following: a series of posters (on an archaeological site or theme), an illustrated guide to the archaeology of a specific place (or museum), a web blog on current issues in archaeology or history of ancient art, a film (video) on a specific site or theme, a reconstruction (model or virtual) of an ancient building, or any subject approved by the project coordinator.

HART 401.name: Summer Practice II
HART 401.description: A course in which the student is expected to take part in actual field work preferably on an excavation or in a museum; other options possible, with approval from department. A report of performance to be submitted to the Department by the supervisor of the field project.

HART 403.name: Greek Sanctuaries
HART 403.description: This course examines the religious, political and social uses of one of the most important institutions of the Greek world, together with the architecture, sculpture, pottery and offerings found in sanctuaries.

HART 409.name: Museum Practices and the Preservation of Cultural Heritage
HART 409.description: Study of various aspects of museum work. Management principles, cataloging and care of art objects, exhibitions and acquisitions, administrative procedures, and museum architecture will be emphasized. Specialist lecturers and visits to museums and their facilities.

HART 410.name: Special Topics in Art, Architecture and Archaeology
HART 410.description: This course provides specialized teaching for a specific in art, architecture and archaeology. In each semester, the topic is chosen by the instructor to highlight a particular theoretical approach and/or regional and chronological focus. The topics chosen aim to train students in contemporary issues in the field, as well as to provide venues for interdisciplinary thinking.

HART 415.name: Ceramics for Field Archaeologists
HART 415.description: HART 415 is a one-week intensive introduction to ceramic analysis for field archaeologists. The course will include lecture sessions on the staples of ceramic analysis such as identifying technologies of production, surface treatment, fabric, ware, form and date. These lectures will be coupled with hands-on work on real archaeological assemblages collected through fieldwork, as well as guided use of digital tools for ceramic research and documentation. HART 415 will also provide an introduction to advanced tools and resources for ceramic studies, including principles of archaeometric analyses. Ultimately, the course aims to enable the students to devise research programs for robust ceramic analyses in their future fieldwork.

HART 420.name: Readings in Prehistory
HART 420.description: Senior seminar on current debates in prehistory, with topic to be set by the instructor.

HART 423.name: Anatolia III-Life in Greek and Roman Anatolia (Classical Anatolia)
HART 423.description: Scattered throughout the modern Republic of Turkey, ancient Anatolia, are the very visible remains of some 100 and more sites and monuments that help illuminate the history and in particular the architectural developments of the Classical period in this region. This course will examine several of these sites and their hinterlands to explain what we can learn from the archaeological remains about changing social and economic systems in the Classical period, roughly 600 BC - AD 300. The course takes a chronological approach to the subject, so that developments in contemporary social and economic systems can be explored and explained at the individual sites. As such, a particular emphasis is placed on how the architectural remains at such sites help us understand their varying degrees of prosperity in the Classical period. However, although the course will naturally focus mainly on such well-known places as Priene, Pergamum and Ephesus, it will also examine what can be learnt from the remains at several less-well known sites, like Patara, Oinoanda, and Ankara.

HART 424.name: Religion and Society in the Ancient Near East
HART 424.description: This course will examine formal and private religion practiced by the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia, the eastern Mediterranean, Anatolia and Egypt. Topics to be covered include religious settings (temples, shrines and outdoor cult places), iconography referring to deities and cults, and ancient texts that explain cult practices and religious beliefs. Lectures, class discussions and student presentations.

HART 426.name: Ancient Technologies and Materials
HART 426.description: This course aims to provide students with a general understanding of the natural sciences (mainly chemistry and physics) contribution to enhance traditional archaeological methodologies. Issues like 14C-dating and Dendrochronology will be in focus as well as Sediment Analysis, X-Ray, lead Isotope- and Spectral Analysis, Laser-Raman-Spectroscopy and FTIR-Spectroscopy. The second part of this course is then devoted to ancient technological innovations and advances in engineering, and their contribution to contemporary materials science.

HART 428.name: Aegean Bronze Age Civilizations
HART 428.description: A survey of the Bronze Age cultures of Greece and Aegean Turkey, with emphasis on the Minoans (Crete), the Cycladic Islands, and the Mycenaeans (mainland Greece).

HART 430.name: Readings in Near Eastern Art and Archaeology
HART 430.description: This course will investigate the most recent issues and scholarship on a topic in the field of Near Eastern art and archaeology. Subject to be announced in the schedule of classes.

HART 431.name: The Archaeology of Cyprus in the Bronze Age
HART 431.description: This course will introduce the richly textured cultures of Cyprus during the Bronze Age (ca. 3500-1100 BC), when the island's resources and advantageous location encouraged interaction with neighbors from the Mediterranean, the Aegean and beyond. Aspects of Cypriot archaeological culture, social organization, technology, and maritime economy will be examined in class lectures, discussions and student presentations.

HART 433.name: The Eastern Roman Provinces
HART 433.description: A detailed and regionally focussed study of the history and architecture of Anatolia and the Levantine zone in the period the relevant areas came under the control of Rome from the earliest days to the beginning of Late Antiquity (ca AD 300-400). Settlements and their architecture will be examined in their political, military, economic and cultural context.

HART 434.name: Landscape Archaeology
HART 434.description: This course offers an in-depth introduction to a major branch of today's archaeology that involves the investigation of ancient landscapes and the dynamics of human-environment interaction across time. Topics include discussion regarding the Anthropocene, resilience theory, political ecology, human-driven environmental and climatic change, sensory archaeology, palaeoclimatology and geoarchaeology, remote sensing and GIS-led landscape analysis.

HART 435.name: Selected Topics in Anatolian Art and Archaeology
HART 435.description: Weekly 3-hour seminar with assigned readings, reports and a research paper on a specialized topic to be selected by the instructor. It will cover specific cultural periods, regions or issues in Anatolian Art and Archaeology.

HART 436.name: Archaeological Method and Theory
HART 436.description: This course discusses analytical approaches that are fundamental to the discipline of archaeology. It will focus on the sequence of major interpretive models that have directed archaeological practice since its emergence as a scientific discipline in the 19th century.

HART 439.name: Neolithic and Chalcolithic Periods in Anatolia
HART 439.description: An examination of the aceramic Neolithic cultures of Southeast Anatolia and the ceramic Neolithic cultures of the South and Southwest Anatolian plateau and their Chalcolithic successors.

HART 440.name: Readings in Anatolian Art and Archaeology
HART 440.description: This course will investigate the most recent issues and scholarship on a topic in the field of Anatolian art and archaeology. Subject to be announced in the schedule of classes.

HART 441.name: Gender and Body Language in Greek and Roman Sculpture
HART 441.description: This course examines in detail the salient features of classical statuary, from the Archaic period to Late Antiquity, within the central theme of gender and body language. After initially focussing on the divine, classical statuary expanded to include real persons. Whether of the divine or of the great, alive or dead, it often personified ideals and role models for contemporary society, and in particular the ways of expressing female and male sexuality.

HART 450.name: Readings in Greek Art and Archaeology
HART 450.description: This course will investigate the most recent issues and scholarship on a topic in the field of Greek art and archaeology. Subject to be announced in the schedule of classes.

HART 453.name: Palaeolithic Archaeology in Eurasia and the Near East
HART 453.description: The science of our ancestors' most ancient cultural period (ca. 1.000.000 - 10.000 BCE) is tremendously dynamic branch of archeology, with an ever-growing body of new, sensational insights into the dawn of man, its dispersal, biological and socio cultural evolution. This seminar is designed to make students familiar with prominent finds and features of the Eurasian and Near Eastern Palaeolithic. Topics include lithic and bone working technologies, artwork, and the archaeology of caves and open air shelters. special attention will be eaually paid to the contribution of neighbouring sciences (Geology, Geochemistry, Palaezoology and -anthropology, Genetics) to reconstruct a more comprehensive picture ofour earliest past.

HART 454.name: Introduction to Sumerology
HART 454.description: The course is an introduction to the study of Sumerian language, documents, history and culture. A history of the discovery of the Sumerian civilization is followed by an overview of Sumerian history and the main features of Sumerian society. The course familiarizes students with the corpus of Sumerian texts in the fields of literature, mythology, religion, economy and political history. The significance of Sumerology for other fields of study, especially Assyriology and Hititology, is explained. The question of Sumerian origins is explored alongside an assessment of the role of the Sumerians in the history of civilizations.

HART 460.name: Readings in Roman Art and Archaeology
HART 460.description: This course will investigate the most recent issues and scholarship on a topic in the field of Roman art and archaeology. Subject to be announced in the schedule of classes.

HART 470.name: Readings in Byzantine Art and Archaeology
HART 470.description: This course will investigate the most recent issues and scholarship on a topic in the field of Byzantine art and archaeology. Subject to be announced in the schedule of classes.

HART 474.name: Neo-Assyrian Art and Archaeology
HART 474.description: The Neo-Assyrian Empire (10th-7th century BC) represents a high moment in the long history of Ancient Near Eastern civilizations. This course covers notable aspects of its architecture, arts and settlement systems as preserved in the archaeological record.

HART 490.name: Supervised Study
HART 490.description: Independent research under the supervision of a faculty member whose special competence coincides with the area of a student's interest. Consent of the supervising faculty member and of the major advisor is required.

HART 491.name: Readings from Near Eastern Texts
HART 491.description: This course will focus on the translation of Near Eastern texts. Knowledge of Akkadian will be a prerequisite.

HART 492.name: Readings From Greek/Latin Texts
HART 492.description: This course will focus on selected readings from original sources.

HART 494.name: Readings From Greek/Latin Texts II
HART 494.description: Reading ancient Greek or Latin authors in their original language. This course requires familiarity with the ancient language beyond the department's 2-year ancient language curriculum.

HART 501.name: Issues in Archaeological Theory
HART 501.description: This course will examine contemporary debates in archaeological methodology, analysis and interpretation. Emphasis will be placed on the techniques for applying theoretical models to fieldwork and analytical research.

HART 503.name: Issues in Conservation and Preservation
HART 503.description: The course aims to study the problems and the solutions related to the conservation and the preservation of the natural and cultural heritage, tangible and intangible. The ethics of restoration and conservation will be discussed, as well as the case of the sites in the conflict or natural disaster zones. Case-studies will be chosen in Turkey as well as in other developed or developing countries.

HART 507.name: Pre-Classical Art and Archaeology
HART 507.description: These classes will be conducted with readings and discussion on key issues of Anatolian art and archaeology from the Prehistoric period to the Iron Age.

HART 508.name: Issues in Pre-Classical Art and Archaeology
HART 508.description: These classes will be conducted with readings and discussion on key issues of Anatolian art and archaeology from the Prehistoric period to the Iron Age.

HART 509.name: Classical Art and Archaeology
HART 509.description: Classes conducted with readings and discussion on key issues of Anatolian art and archaeology from the Greek, Hellenistic and Roman periods.

HART 510.name: Issues in Classical Art and Archaeology
HART 510.description: Classes conducted with readings and discussion on key issues of Anatolian art and archaeology from the Greek, Hellenistic and Roman periods.

HART 514.name: Readings in Classical Archaeology
HART 514.description: Graduate tutorial in Classical Archaeology, on a topic to be chosen by the instructor.

HART 515.name: Readings in Near Eastern Archaeology
HART 515.description: Graduate tutorial in Near Eastern Archaeology, on a topic to be chosen by the instructor.

HART 516.name: Supervised Research in Near Eastern Archaeology
HART 516.description: Independent study, on a topic relevant to the student's specialized research field in Near Eastern archaeology.

HART 517.name: Readings in Anatolian Archaeology
HART 517.description: Graduate tutorial in Anatolian Archaeology, on a topic to be chosen by the instructor.

HART 518.name: Supervised Research in Anatolian Archaeology
HART 518.description: Independent study, on a topic relevant to the student's specialized research field in Anatolian archaeology.

HART 519.name: Research Directions for Anatolian Archaeology and Art
HART 519.description: A team-taught pro-seminar to introduce research perspectives and sources, with one topic per week, on periods (Neolithic, Ancient Near East and Egypt, Iron Age Near East, Bronze Age Europe/Mediterranean, Greece, Rome, Byzantium, Islamic world) and themes (Science in Archeology, Ancient Languages and Epigraphy, Ethnoarcheology, Ceramics and Artefactual Analyses).

HART 521.name: Problems in Medieval Art and Archaeology
HART 521.description: Classes conducted with readings and discussion on key issues of Anatolian art and archaeology of the Byzantine, Islamic, Seljuk and Ottoman periods.

HART 523.name: Medieval Art and Archaeology
HART 523.description: Classes conducted with readings and discussion on key issues of Anatolian art and archaeology of the Byzantine, Islamic, Seljuk and Ottoman periods.

HART 524.name: Issues in Medieval Art and Archaeology
HART 524.description: Classes conducted with readings and discussion on key issues of Anatolian art and archaeology of the Byzantine, Islamic, Seljuk and Ottoman periods.

HART 531.name: Ceramics for Field Archaeologists
HART 531.description: HART 531 is a one-week intensive introduction to ceramic analysis for field archaeologists. The course will include lecture sessions on the staples of ceramic analysis such as identifying technologies of production, surface treatment, fabric, ware, form and date. These lectures will be coupled with hands-on work on real archaeological assemblages collected through fieldwork, as well as guided use of digital tools for ceramic research and documentation. HART 531 will also provide an introduction to advanced tools and resources for ceramic studies, including principles of archaeometric analyses. Ultimately, the course aims to enable the students to devise research programs for robust ceramic analyses in their future fieldwork.

HART 542.name: Hittite I
HART 542.description: An introduction to Hittite, the oldest attested Indo-European language. Overview of the discovery of the Hittite language and civilization, and presentation of the basics of Hittite grammar and cuneiform script.

HART 543.name: Hittite II
HART 543.description: A detailed survey of Hittite grammar and orthography. Beginner level excerpts from Hittite texts read and analyzed.

HART 544.name: Hittite III
HART 544.description: This course will offer a survey of the Hittite textual corpus. Students will read and translate selected historical and religious texts.

HART 545.name: Hittite IV
HART 545.description: This course will further explore the Hittite text corpus. Students will read and translate selected literary texts.

HART 546.name: Akkadian I
HART 546.description: An introduction to the Akkadian language, attested in writing in Mesopotamia from the mid-third millennium BCE until the early first millennium CE. Akkadian was the lingua franca of much of the Ancient Near East in the 2nd millennium BCE and the language of such important compositions as the Code of Hammurabi and the Epic of Gilgamesh. The course will cover the basics of Akkadian (Old Babylonian) grammar and the cuneiform script.

HART 547.name: Akkadian II
HART 547.description: Continuation of Akkadian I, with emphasis on developing reading skills.

HART 551.name: Ancient Greek I
HART 551.description: Introduction to ancient Greek for beginning students. The course will emphasize vocabulary acquisition grammar and reading.

HART 552.name: Ancient Greek II
HART 552.description: Continuation of the grammar and vocabulary acquisition started in Ancient Greek I.

HART 553.name: Ancient Greek III
HART 553.description: Completion of the grammar and vocabulary acquisition started in Ancient Greek I and II.

HART 554.name: Ancient Greek IV
HART 554.description: Selections from Greek literature, and an introduction to epigraphy.

HART 563.name: Latin I
HART 563.description: Introduction to Latin for graduate students. Basic points of grammar will be covered and reading skills developed.

HART 564.name: Latin II
HART 564.description: Continuation of the grammar and development of reading skills introduced in Latin I.

HART 576.name: The Land of a Thousand Gods: History and Literature of Ancient Anatolia
HART 576.description: This course will survey the history and literature of early Anatolian civilizations such as the Hittites, Phrygians, and Urartians, from the Early Bronze Age (c. 3000 BCE) to the end of the Persian Period (c. 330 BCE). Students will explore the history of Anatolia through a diverse range of theoretical lectures and hands-on activities: reading and interpreting primary sources (myths, annals, treaties, letters, etc.) in English translation, visiting museums and archaeological sites, or participating in workshops on ancient writing techniques.

HART 583.name: Latin III
HART 583.description: Selections from Latin literature and an introduction to epigraphy.

HART 584.name: Latin IV
HART 584.description: Selections from Latin literature, prose composition, and an introduction to numismatics.

HART 588.name: Readings From Greek/Latin Texts
HART 588.description: Reading ancient Greek or Latin authors in their original language. This course requires familiarity with the ancient language beyond the department's 2-year ancient language curriculum.

HART 590.name: Seminar
HART 590.description: A seminar on research topics in archaeology.

HART 599.name: Master's Thesis
HART 599.description: A research-based thesis on an individual project. Timely, relevant and substantial research on a topic in the general area of Eastern Mediterranean archaeology, focusing preferably on Anatolian archaeology (prehistory, Bronze-Iron Ages, classical, medieval). Topic to be agreed in consultation with the Thesis advisor.
